source_refs.note: Topic 9.3 with Table 9.2, printed pages 192-193. The printed Kw exponents (10^14) are read as 10^-14 and noted.

blocks.text: Pure water is a poor conductor of electricity, but its conductance is measurable because water undergoes self-ionisation reversibly: H2O(l) + H2O(l) gives H3O+(aq) + OH-(aq), or as a net reaction H2O(l) gives H+(aq) + OH-(aq). The equilibrium constant is Kc = [H+][OH-] / [H2O] = 1.8 x 10^-16 mol dm-3. The concentration of water in pure water is 1000 g dm-3 divided by 18 g mol-1, giving 55.5 mol dm-3; since water is present in very large excess and very few of its molecules ionise, its concentration remains effectively constant. This constant concentration is taken to the left-hand side and multiplied with Kc to give another constant, Kw: Kc [H2O] = [H+][OH-], or 1.8 x 10^-16 x 55.5 = 1.01 x 10^-14 = [H+][OH-]. This 1.01 x 10^-14 is Kw, the ionic product of water or dissociation constant of water, at 25 degrees C: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10^-14 at 25 degrees C. The value of Kw increases almost 75 times when the temperature is raised from 0 to 100 degrees C.

For neutral water [H+] = [OH-], so [H+]^2 = 10^-14 at 25 degrees C and [H+] = 10^-7 mol dm-3 and [OH-] = 10^-7 mol dm-3. Whenever some acid or base is added to water, Kw remains the same but [H+] and [OH-] are no longer equal: with a small amount of acid [H+] is greater than [OH-], and with a few drops of base [OH-] is greater than [H+]. During both additions Kw remains 10^-14 at 25 degrees C.
